paras: The attempted lynching of Daniel Wagner took place on Sunday, March 12, 1882, in Park Place, Scranton, Pennsylvania, when a crowd surrounded a barn where Wagner, a fifty-five-year-old man accused of assaulting an eight-year-old girl, was hiding. Wagner was arrested and jailed, and no one was reported hurt. The papers carried the episode only as a brief wire dispatch, and none of them identified Wagner's race.

According to the dispatch dated at Scranton on March 12, Wagner "hod committed an outmgo on nn clgfit-ycar-old girl," and had concealed himself in the barn of a man named "Grifflns" in Park Place. A crowd "with the intent of lynching" surrounded the barn. The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer's version said the crowd had gathered "for the purpose of lynching" Wagner, "who had feloniously assaulted a little girl."
Wagner was arrested and committed to jail in default of $1,000 bail. The Cambria Freeman, an Ebensburg weekly, described the arrest instead as a rescue: "He was rescued by officers and sent to jail."
No report of arrests among the crowd, or of a hearing or trial for Wagner, appears in the coverage.

The Washington National Republican printed the fullest form of the dispatch on March 13, among its telegraph items under a garbled headline. The same day the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and the Daily Gazette ran an identical one-sentence condensation in their crime and general-news briefs. Weeklies repeated it later in the week, the Cambria Freeman on March 17 with its own wording and the Westminster, Maryland, Democratic Advocate on March 18 as a reprint of the shorter brief.
Every version stated the accusation against Wagner as fact and offered no comment on the crowd's purpose. None mentioned race, and the item ran alongside unrelated accounts of crimes and accidents.

bases: A crowd surrounded the barn where Wagner was hiding with the stated purpose of lynching him, and officers arrested him and took him to jail (A1, A3, A4).

A crowd gathered to lynch Wagner over an accusation of assaulting a girl, but no one was killed: he was arrested, or 'rescued by officers', and jailed (A1, A3, A4), so this was an attempted lynching, not a completed one.

All four reports appear to derive from one Scranton dispatch of March 12 (A1 carries the dateline; A2, A3 and A4 are condensed versions of it); no local Scranton paper or independent account was found.
